chapter_summary:
Network connectivity and performance issues are among the most frequent and challenging problems faced by system administrators. A systematic approach is essential, starting from the physical layer and moving up the OSI model. Begin by verifying physical connectivity: check cables, network interface card (NIC) status (`ip link show`), and switch port status. Next, confirm IP address configuration (`ip addr show`), subnet mask, and default gateway (`ip route show`). A common mistake is an incorrect subnet mask, which prevents communication with hosts on the same logical network, or a misconfigured default gateway, which isolates the system from external networks. Tools like `ping` and `traceroute` (`mtr` is often preferred for more detailed diagnostics) are fundamental for testing reachability and identifying where traffic stops. `ping` checks basic IP connectivity, while `traceroute` maps the path packets take, helping to pinpoint routing issues or intermediate device failures.

Once basic IP connectivity is established, focus shifts to DNS resolution. Many applications rely heavily on DNS, and a failure here can mimic network connectivity problems. Check the `/etc/resolv.conf` file for correct DNS server entries. Use `dig` or `nslookup` to test DNS resolution for specific hostnames. `dig google.com @8.8.8.8` can test a specific DNS server directly, bypassing local resolvers. If DNS resolution fails, verify the DNS server itself is reachable and functioning. Incorrect entries in `/etc/hosts` can also override DNS, leading to unexpected resolution. For more persistent issues, `systemd-resolve --status` provides detailed information about `systemd-resolved` if it's in use.

Advanced network analysis involves deeper inspection of network traffic and connections. `ss` (socket statistics) is the modern replacement for `netstat` and provides more detailed information about open ports, established connections, and socket statistics. `ss -tunlp` shows all TCP and UDP listening sockets and established connections, along with the process ID (PID) and program name. This is invaluable for identifying which process is using a specific port or if a service is listening on the wrong interface. For capturing and analyzing network packets, `tcpdump` is an incredibly powerful tool. `tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.100 and port 80` will capture all traffic on `eth0` to or from `192.168.1.100` on port 80. Analyzing `tcpdump` output can reveal dropped packets, retransmissions, TCP handshake failures, or application-level protocol issues. Safety note: `tcpdump` can generate large amounts of data quickly; use filters judiciously to avoid overwhelming the system or capturing sensitive information unnecessarily.

Firewall rules are a frequent cause of perceived network issues. `iptables` (or `nftables` on newer systems) can block legitimate traffic if misconfigured. Use `sudo iptables -L -nv` to list all current `iptables` rules with packet and byte counts, which helps identify if traffic is hitting a specific rule. Similarly, `sudo nft list ruleset` for `nftables`. A common mistake is to add rules without saving them, leading to them being lost on reboot, or to add overly restrictive rules that block necessary services. Always test firewall changes in a controlled environment and have a rollback plan. For performance issues, `iperf3` can measure network bandwidth between two hosts, helping to distinguish between network capacity issues and application-layer bottlenecks. `netstat -s` or `ss -s` can show network statistics, including error counts. `sar -n DEV 1` provides real-time network interface statistics, showing utilization and packet rates. By combining these tools and following a methodical approach, even complex network problems can be systematically diagnosed and resolved.

screens.title: Network Connectivity & Performance Problems
screens.subtitle: A stepwise approach to find why hosts can’t talk or are slow

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn a practical, layered method to find and fix network connectivity and performance problems on Linux. We begin at the physical link and move upward through IP configuration, routing, DNS, socket state, packet captures, firewall rules, and performance measurement. You will see concrete command-line patterns that reveal where traffic stops, which service is listening, and whether a firewall or DNS misconfiguration is to blame. For example, a mis-set subnet mask can isolate two hosts on the same switch even though the cable and NIC appear functional. You will practice interpreting simple tcpdump captures, reading ss output to find listening processes, and using iperf3 to decide if the network, rather than the application, is the bottleneck. This chapter matters because most production outages follow a predictable path: link, addressing, name resolution, service binding, then firewall or performance limits. By the end you will be able to pick the right tool for each layer and sequence checks so troubleshooting is fast and repeatable. Think about a recent time you had to wait for a service to respond — this chapter turns that frustration into a repeatable diagnostic workflow.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use a systematic, OSI-inspired order of checks and the right Linux tools so you identify whether the problem is physical, addressing, DNS, services, firewall, or capacity.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will apply a repeatable troubleshooting sequence and use concrete Linux commands to isolate faults. First, you will learn to start at the physical and link layer, reading NIC state and switch port clues so you avoid chasing software symptoms when the cable or link is the real cause. Second, you will interpret IP configuration and routing so you can tell when a bad subnet mask or missing default gateway prevents external traffic. Third, you will become proficient with DNS checks so name-resolution failures no longer masquerade as network outages. Fourth, you will practice socket and packet inspection to discover whether a service is listening correctly and whether packets are dropped or retransmitted. Each objective pairs a command pattern with the reasoning behind it so you not only run checks but understand the signal each output provides. These skills let you move confidently through incidents and build hypotheses that you can test quickly. You will also get hands-on practice reproducing and resolving a blocked web connection to solidify the workflow.

screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting sequence
screens.subtitle: How to move from link checks to capacity testing without guessing

narration.text: Effective troubleshooting begins with a predictable sequence that reduces wasted effort and prevents misdirected fixes. Treat the network as layers: first confirm physical and link layer health, then verify IP addressing and routing, next validate DNS and name resolution, then check sockets and services, review firewall rules, and finally measure capacity if performance is poor. This sequence matters because a failing cable or wrong subnet mask will produce symptoms that look like a service or DNS problem, so correcting the wrong layer wastes time. For example, if two hosts on the same switch cannot communicate, a quick ip addr show and ip route show will reveal a mismatched subnet mask or missing route. After you confirm addressing, use ping to test basic reachability and traceroute or mtr to identify where packets stop. If reachability is confirmed but applications fail, test name resolution with dig or nslookup to rule out DNS. Once address and name checks pass, examine sockets with ss and capture traffic with tcpdump to observe whether packets reach the host and whether TCP handshakes complete. Only after these steps should you test bandwidth with iperf3. A common misconception is to start by changing firewall rules immediately; resist that until you know which layer blocks the traffic. End each investigation by removing temporary rules and documenting the root cause.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Follow layers: Link → Addressing → Name → Service → Firewall → Capacity to efficiently narrow root cause.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › A systematic troubleshooting sequence
Core Concept

Layered Diagnostic Steps

A numbered process reduces false positives and keeps changes minimal during incidents.

  1. 1. Physical/link: cables, NIC status, switch port.
  2. 2. IP config and routing: ip addr show, ip route show.
  3. 3. Reachability: ping, traceroute, mtr.
  4. 4. DNS: resolv.conf, dig, systemd-resolve if used.
  5. 5. Services & sockets: ss -tunlp and process mapping.
  6. 6. Packet capture: tcpdump with focused filters.
  7. 7. Firewall: iptables -L -nv or nft list ruleset.
  8. 8. Capacity: iperf3 and interface stats.
Key Takeaway

Use order to avoid changing the wrong thing and make every change reversible for quick rollback.

Process visual
Commands & checks
ip link show
ip addr show
ip route show
ping 
traceroute 
dig example.com
ss -tunlp
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.10 and port 80
sudo iptables -L -nv
iperf3 -s  # on server
iperf3 -c   # on client
Concrete example
If ping works but curl to a web server times out, check DNS and then sockets. If sockets show the service listening, verify firewall counters and capture packets to confirm drops.
Common mistake
Jumping to firewall changes before confirming addressing often causes wasted change windows. Always form a hypothesis first.
Check your understanding
Name a single failing output that would move you from step 2 to step 4 without modifying anything in between.

screens.title: Link-layer and NIC verification
screens.subtitle: Read NIC state and interpret common link symptoms

narration.text: Start every network investigation by confirming the physical and link layers. On Linux, ip link show reveals whether an interface is UP and whether it has carrier. A downed interface often shows as state DOWN or lacks the LOWER_UP flag; that is a clue to cable, switch, or NIC driver problems. Check switch port LEDs and confirm the NIC driver has loaded in the kernel. Another quick sign is mismatched speed or duplex settings that cause drops and retransmissions; these often show up as high error counts in interface statistics. If you see no carrier, do not proceed to application debugging — replace the cable or check the virtual switch configuration first. For virtual machines, check the hypervisor virtual NIC state. A useful command is to monitor interface counters over time. Persistently rising error, drop, or collision counts point to link issues rather than routing or DNS. An easy mistake is assuming a green link LED always means healthy; it only indicates physical layer presence, not correct configuration or driver-level problems. The correct sequence is: identify the interface name, check ip link, examine counters, and confirm physical or virtual switch state before moving upward.

keyIdea.title: Link check
keyIdea.text: Confirm interface UP and carrier, then inspect counters for drops and errors before moving to IP-level checks.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Link-layer and NIC verification
Definition

Confirm physical and link health

Interpret interface state and counters so you can confidently rule in or out layer-1/2 faults.

# Inspect link state and flags
ip link show eth0

# View counters and errors
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/statistics/rx_errors
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/statistics/tx_dropped

# Watch statistics over time (example)
sar -n DEV 1 5
Concrete scenario
A VM shows no carrier: check hypervisor vNIC mapping. Reattach or restart the virtual NIC rather than reconfiguring IPs.
Misconception
A green LED is not proof of correct settings; duplex or driver issues still cause packet errors.
Quick checks and visuals
Interpretation tips
  • LOWER_UP indicates physical carrier; absence means no link.
  • Rising error counters suggest physical or NIC driver issues.
  • Consistent drops during bursts suggest duplex mismatch or faulty cable.
Check your understanding
If ip link shows UP and carrier but you still see Rx errors, what is the likely next check? (Answer: driver and duplex/speed mismatch or faulty switch port.)
Key Takeaway
Physical validation prevents wasted application-level debugging. Always confirm link and counters first.

screens.title: IP configuration and routing
screens.subtitle: Understand ip addr and ip route outputs and common mistakes

narration.text: After the link is validated, inspect IP configuration and routing. The ip addr show command lists addresses assigned to interfaces, their prefixes, and whether they are tentative or permanent. A frequent problem is a wrong subnet mask that keeps two hosts on the same switch from communicating, because each host thinks the other is on a different network. ip route show reveals default gateways and routing table entries; missing or incorrect default routes isolate the host from external networks. When you see multiple interfaces with addresses, ensure the service listens on the correct interface. Also check for unexpected virtual bridges or containers that add competing IP space. A common mistake is to assign an IP manually without updating the route or to rely on DHCP that failed silently. Use simple checks: ping the gateway, ping another host on the same subnet, and run ip route get to see how the kernel would route to a destination. These steps quickly confirm whether the kernel-level routing matches your expectation and whether the issue is local configuration rather than external network devices. IP configuration and routing means ip addr and ip route outputs reveal whether addressing and kernel routing align with network design and expected reachability.. In practical terms, understand ip addr and ip route outputs and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Routing insight
keyIdea.text: ip addr and ip route outputs reveal whether addressing and kernel routing align with network design and expected reachability.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › IP configuration and routing
Definition

IP addresses and kernel routing

Verify assigned addresses, prefixes, and the default route so packets go where you expect.

# Show addresses
ip addr show

# Show routing table
ip route show

# Simulate kernel routing decision
ip route get 8.8.8.8
Concrete example
Two VMs on same switch cannot reach each other: compare subnet prefixes; a host with /24 and another with /25 may not see each other if addresses fall outside the shared range.
Explanation & pitfalls
  • Missing default gateway prevents external access even if local subnet works.
  • Multiple routes or 0.0.0.0 entries can lead to asymmetric routing and dropped replies.
  • DHCP failures can leave stale or no addresses; validate lease state when applicable.
Pro tip
Use ip route get to see the exact outgoing interface and gateway the kernel picks for a destination.
Key Takeaway
Addressing and routes must align with your network design; mismatches are frequent causes of isolation.

screens.title: Ping, traceroute, and mtr
screens.subtitle: When to use each tool and what their outputs tell you

narration.text: Use reachability tools to locate where traffic stops. Ping is the simplest: it verifies basic IP reachability and round-trip latency; a sequence of lost pings suggests packet loss or filtering. Traceroute maps the hops packets traverse and shows the point where responses time out, which helps locate upstream routing or intermediate device failures. mtr combines these ideas into an iterative, live probe that shows latency and loss over time for each hop, making it more useful for intermittent issues. A common pitfall is assuming traceroute always follows the same path as application traffic; asymmetric routing or load-balanced links can show different paths. Also, some devices rate-limit or drop ICMP responses, giving misleading hop gaps even though TCP traffic might pass. Use traceroute or mtr with the same protocol your application uses if possible, and interpret missing hops as hints rather than absolute proof of outage. After these checks, you should know whether packets leave your host and whether intermediate devices respond — essential facts before checking DNS, services, or firewalls. Ping, traceroute, and mtr means ping checks reachability; traceroute finds path hops; mtr gives continuous hop-level loss and latency to spot intermittent problems.. In practical terms, when to use each tool and what their outputs tell you. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tool contrast
keyIdea.text: Ping checks reachability; traceroute finds path hops; mtr gives continuous hop-level loss and latency to spot intermittent problems.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Ping, traceroute, and mtr
Comparison

Reachability and path tools

Choose the right tool for the symptom: single failure vs. path diagnosis vs. intermittent loss.

Ping
Quick check for IP-layer reachability and baseline latency. Repeated loss often indicates packet drops or filtering.
Traceroute
Maps the sequence of hops and shows where responses stop, useful to locate the problematic device or segment.
mtr
Live, continuous probing that reports per-hop loss and latency over time — ideal for intermittent or variable issues.
Examples & interpretation
Scenario
Ping to server returns replies but HTTP fails. Run traceroute to identify whether packets exit your network and whether responses stop at a particular hop. If traceroute completes but HTTP times out, suspect firewall, service, or socket binding issues.
Pro tip
Use traceroute with TCP probes where possible to emulate application traffic; this avoids false positives from ICMP filtering.
Key Takeaway
Interpret missing traceroute hops cautiously; they are clues, not final proof. Combine results with tcpdump or ss for confirmation.

screens.title: DNS troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Diagnose resolution issues and common misconfigurations

narration.text: DNS problems frequently mimic network outages because applications fail when hostnames don't resolve. Start by checking /etc/resolv. conf for correct nameserver entries; if this file points to an unreachable or wrong server, name lookups fail even though IP paths are fine. Use dig or nslookup to query a specific server and bypass local resolvers, for instance querying a public server to confirm whether the hostname exists. If the system uses systemd-resolved, run systemd-resolve --status to view current resolver configuration and link-level DNS settings. Also inspect /etc/hosts for entries that override DNS and can lead to unexpected resolutions. A useful test is to run dig against a known working DNS server to separate local caching or resolver problems from upstream DNS failures. Be aware that DNS caching, negative caching, or stale entries can persist across tests. A common misconception is to assume that successful ping by IP equals no DNS problem; but many apps use hostnames, so always verify name resolution separately. When DNS is failing, confirm whether the DNS server is reachable and whether recursive resolution is permitted and functioning.

keyIdea.title: DNS check
keyIdea.text: Validate resolv.conf, query a specific DNS server with dig, and inspect systemd-resolved state when present.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › DNS troubleshooting
Definition

Name resolution verification

Separate name resolution failures from IP-level connectivity using targeted queries and resolver inspection.

# Check resolver configuration
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Query a specific server to bypass local view
dig example.com @8.8.8.8

# Inspect systemd-resolved state if present
systemd-resolve --status
Concrete example
If dig to a public resolver returns answers but application lookups fail, investigate local resolver or /etc/hosts overrides.
Common symptoms & remediation
  • Incorrect nameserver IPs in resolv.conf → replace with reachable server and test.
  • /etc/hosts overrides causing unexpected addresses → remove stale entries.
  • systemd-resolved stub resolver issues → check link-specific DNS and restart resolver if needed.
Pro tip
When diagnosing, always query a known-working public DNS to separate local caching from upstream failures.
Key Takeaway
DNS failures can make applications appear offline even when IP connectivity is healthy; verify names explicitly.

screens.title: Inspecting sockets with ss
screens.subtitle: Find which process is listening and where

narration.text: When an application is unreachable despite successful name resolution and ping, inspect sockets to see whether the service is listening. The ss command is the modern replacement for netstat and provides clear output about TCP and UDP sockets, listening ports, and the processes owning them. Running ss -tunlp shows TCP and UDP sockets, listening state, process ID, and program name so you can confirm both port and interface. This helps you spot services bound only to the loopback interface, which will be unreachable from remote hosts, or services listening on the wrong IP. If you do not see a listening socket, verify the service status and logs with systemctl. A common misconception is assuming a running service always listens on the expected port and interface; configuration errors or command-line options can change bind behavior. Use ss output to map the socket to a PID, then examine the process to correct binding settings. This check narrows your troubleshooting to service configuration or host firewall rules rather than network routing. Inspecting sockets with ss means ss -tunlp identifies listening sockets and the owning process to determine whether a service is reachable from the network.. In practical terms, find which process is listening and where. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Socket mapping
keyIdea.text: ss -tunlp identifies listening sockets and the owning process to determine whether a service is reachable from the network.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Inspecting sockets with ss
Core Concept

Socket and process mapping

Confirm which ports are listening and which processes own them to localize service-level problems.

# Show TCP/UDP listening sockets with process info
ss -tunlp

# Filter for port 80
ss -tunlp | grep ':80'
Concrete example
If a web server shows LISTEN on 127.0.0.1:80 but not on 0.0.0.0, it will be inaccessible from other hosts. Reconfigure binding to the correct interface or use a reverse proxy.
Actionable bullets
  • Use ss -tunlp to list sockets and identify PID/program name.
  • If the service is not listening, check systemctl status and the service logs for bind errors.
  • Confirm the service binds to the expected interface and port, not only loopback.
Common mistake
Assuming port availability means process ownership; ephemeral sockets and container networking can obscure expected bindings.
Key Takeaway
ss reveals what the kernel sees. If the socket is absent, focus on service configuration and logs rather than network devices.

screens.title: Capturing traffic with tcpdump
screens.subtitle: Filter effectively and interpret common capture patterns

narration.text: Packet capture is one of the most powerful diagnostics but also one of the most dangerous if used without filters. Tcpdump can show you whether packets arrive at a host, whether TCP handshakes complete, and whether retransmissions occur. Always craft filters to limit capture volume and sensitive data. A typical focused command captures traffic for a single host and port on an interface. Watch for SYN packets without matching SYN-ACKs — that indicates handshake failures, often due to firewall drops. Retransmissions and duplicate ACKs point to packet loss or congestion. Use tcpdump output alongside ss and iptables counters to determine whether packets are being dropped locally or upstream. A practical safety tip: avoid capturing everything on a production system without rotation and ensure capture files are stored securely. A common misconception is that tcpdump will always show application-level protocol details; encrypted traffic or higher-layer issues require correlating timestamps and TCP behavior rather than payload inspection alone. Read tcpdump timestamps, flag patterns, and lengths to build your hypothesis before making changes. Capturing traffic with tcpdump means use narrow tcpdump filters, watch tcp flags for handshake problems, and combine observations with socket and firewall counters.. In practical terms, filter effectively and interpret common capture patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Capture pattern
keyIdea.text: Use narrow tcpdump filters, watch TCP flags for handshake problems, and combine observations with socket and firewall counters.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Capturing traffic with tcpdump
Process Flow

Safe packet capture

Apply focused filters and interpret TCP flags to find handshake failures, retransmits, and drops.

# Capture traffic to or from a host on port 80 on eth0
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.10 and port 80

# Capture only SYN packets to observe handshake attempts
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
Concrete example
Seeing SYNs without SYN-ACKs suggests that packets reach the server interface but responses are blocked or never leave the server. Cross-check iptables counters to confirm.
Interpretation cards
SYN without SYN-ACK
Indicates the server did not respond or replies were dropped; check service, firewall, or routing for return path issues.
Retransmissions
Multiple retransmits and duplicate ACKs point to packet loss or congestion between endpoints.
Key Takeaway
Combine tcpdump with ss and firewall counters to determine whether packets reach the host and whether replies are sent or dropped.

screens.title: Firewalls: iptables and nftables
screens.subtitle: List rules, read counters, and avoid common firewall traps

narration.text: Firewalls are often the unintentional cause of connectivity failures. Inspect rule sets and packet counters to see whether traffic is being matched and dropped. On legacy systems, iptables -L -nv lists chains with packet and byte counters so you can identify rules that are actively dropping or rejecting traffic. On newer systems, nft list ruleset provides the nftables ruleset and counters. A typical troubleshooting pattern is to temporarily add a rule that ACCEPTs traffic from the client IP to the service port and see if connectivity returns, but only do this in a controlled environment with a rollback plan. A common mistake is to add restrictive rules without saving them, meaning the fix is lost after reboot, or to open ports without addressing the root cause. When rules are complex, use packet counters and timestamps to confirm whether a specific rule matches your traffic. Also be aware of default DROP policies and forward chain rules in NAT or bridge environments that can silently block traffic between VMs. Always document and remove temporary rules once testing is complete. Firewalls: iptables and nftables means use rule listings and counters to see whether traffic is matched and dropped; test cautiously with reversible changes.. In practical terms, list rules, read counters, and avoid common firewall traps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Firewall debugging
keyIdea.text: Use rule listings and counters to see whether traffic is matched and dropped; test cautiously with reversible changes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Firewalls: iptables and nftables
Comparison

Inspecting iptables and nftables

List rules and counters to see whether traffic is explicitly dropped or accepted by rules.

# List iptables with counters
sudo iptables -L -nv

# List nftables ruleset
sudo nft list ruleset
Concrete example
An INPUT rule dropping packets from the client IP will show non-zero packet counters; remove or adjust that rule to restore access and then document the change.
Practical notes
  • Look for packet counters in rule listing to see active matches.
  • Test changes in a maintenance window or with a rollback; many mistakes are caused by overly broad rules.
  • Remember to persist intentional rule changes so they survive reboot if desired.
Common mistake
Adding temporary ACCEPT rules and forgetting to remove them adds risk. Always record and revert test rules after validation.
Key Takeaway
Firewall counters are diagnostic gold; use them to prove whether packets are being matched and dropped.

screens.title: Measuring performance and capacity
screens.subtitle: Distinguish network bottlenecks from application limits

narration.text: When connectivity is present but performance is poor, measure network capacity before changing application settings. iperf3 runs a sender and receiver test to report achievable bandwidth and helps you determine whether the network or the application is the bottleneck. Set one host to iperf3 server mode and run the client from the other host to get a clear throughput measurement. In addition, use system counters like ss -s or netstat -s to inspect TCP errors, retransmissions, and socket queues. sar -n DEV 1 shows interface utilization and packet rates over time, revealing sustained congestion. A common trap is assuming application slowness means the network is at fault; application-level resource exhaustion, poor thread pools, or slow storage can also cause slowness even when iperf3 reports high throughput. Run iperf3 tests during similar load patterns and interpret results in context: a lower-than-expected throughput suggests a network constraint, while normal throughput combined with slow application responses points to the application stack. Document test results and repeat them after configuration changes to validate improvements. Measuring performance and capacity means use iperf3 to measure raw throughput and system counters to detect tcp-level errors and interface saturation.. In practical terms, distinguish network bottlenecks from application limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use iperf3 to measure raw throughput and system counters to detect TCP-level errors and interface saturation.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Measuring performance and capacity
Process Flow

Bandwidth and interface statistics

Measure network throughput and TCP-level errors to locate capacity limits.

# Start iperf3 on server
iperf3 -s

# Run client test from another host
iperf3 -c 

# Interface statistics over time
sar -n DEV 1 5

# TCP statistics summary
ss -s
Concrete example
Iperf3 shows 900 Mbps on a gig network, so if the application is slow, focus on the application stack rather than the network.
Interpretation
  • Low iperf3 throughput indicates a network bottleneck — check link, NIC offload, and switch configs.
  • High retransmits in ss -s suggest packet loss and may explain poor application performance despite apparent bandwidth.
  • Combine measurements with tcpdump to locate where loss occurs.
Pro tip
Run iperf3 with similar parallel streams and durations to match application patterns for a realistic test.
Key Takeaway
Measure before changing: iperf3 and interface stats tell you whether to optimize network or application layers.

screens.title: Lab scenario: web server unreachable
screens.subtitle: Diagnose between two VMs: client 192.168.1.20 and server 192.168.1.10

narration.text: In this hands-on scenario you will reproduce a common troubleshooting workflow. Two VMs on the same network segment are configured: VM1 the client at 192.168.1.20 and VM2 the server at 192.168.1.10. The web server is installed and should listen on port 80. First, confirm NIC and link on both VMs with ip link show and check ip addr show to ensure addresses are present. Next, from the client run ping to the server to verify basic connectivity. If ping works but curl hangs, check ss on the server to see if the web server listens on the correct interface. Then simulate a firewall block on the server using iptables to drop traffic from the client IP to port 80 and observe client behavior: curl should hang or time out. While the client attempts curl, capture traffic with tcpdump on the server to see incoming SYNs and whether replies are sent. Finally, list iptables with counters to observe matched packets and remove the blocking rule to restore access. This exercise teaches correlation: link and addressing checks, socket inspection, firewall counters, and packet captures together prove the cause and confirm the fix.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Reproduce the problem, confirm reachability, inspect sockets, capture packets, verify firewall counters, remove the rule, and re-test.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Lab: web server unreachable
Hands-on Activity

Diagnose two VMs

Follow these scripted checks to prove cause and verification steps for the outage.

Server checks
Confirm Nginx is running, verify listening ports with ss -tunlp, and prepare tcpdump on the server to capture client traffic to port 80.
Client checks
Ping the server and run curl to observe timeout. Use traceroute if ping fails to locate the hop where traffic stops.
Simulated block
On the server add a temporary iptables rule to drop traffic from the client IP and watch tcpdump to see SYNs arriving without responses. Then check iptables counters to prove match.
Command callouts
# On server: check service and listening sockets
sudo systemctl status nginx
ss -tunlp | grep 80

# Simulate block on server
sudo iptables -A INPUT -s 192.168.1.20 -p tcp --dport 80 -j DROP
sudo iptables -L -nv

# On client: test and capture
ping 192.168.1.10
curl http://192.168.1.10  # will hang if blocked
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.10 and port 80  # run while curling

# On server: remove block
sudo iptables -D INPUT -s 192.168.1.20 -p tcp --dport 80 -j DROP
Key Takeaway
A coordinated set of checks across client and server proves whether the cause is network, DNS, firewall, or service configuration.

narration.text: Keep a small set of core ideas in mind when troubleshooting networks. First, use a layered approach inspired by the OSI model to reduce misdiagnosis. Second, the ip command family is your primary interface to inspect addresses, interfaces, and routing; learn to read ip addr and ip route clearly. Third, reachability tools like ping and traceroute give quick clues about where packets stop; mtr is useful when behavior changes over time. These three concepts cover most initial investigations and help you choose deeper tools when necessary. Remember: testing in a controlled, reversible way is safer than making broad changes. Keep comparing outputs and documenting steps so you can return the system to its prior state if needed. Finally, always document changes, test reversibility, and confirm the fix by repeating the initial failing request. These habits make troubleshooting faster and safer in production environments.
